relationship: Divine creation of all things
rationale: Sirach attributes the creation of all things to the one who lives for ever; Wisdom's prayer likewise addresses God as the maker of all things, expressly adding creation by His word.

relationship: Divine vindication
rationale: Sirach declares that the Lord alone will be justified; Romans contrasts God's truth with human falsehood and quotes the declaration that God is justified in His words.

relationship: Unsearchable divine works
rationale: Sirach denies human ability to declare or trace God's mighty works fully; Job calls His great works unsearchable and beyond numbering.

relationship: Divine greatness and mercy beyond measure
rationale: Sirach asks who can count God's greatness and recount His mercies; the psalm describes His greatness as without limit and His mercy as abundant while recounting His mighty acts.

relationship: Nothing added to or removed from God's work
rationale: Both passages deny the possibility of adding to or diminishing what God has done. Ecclesiastes additionally states that His work endures for ever.

relationship: Question about the human being's significance
rationale: Sirach asks what a human being is and what use or good belongs to him; the psalm asks what a human being is that God remembers and visits him.

relationship: Contrasting estimates of a bounded human lifespan
rationale: Sirach describes a hundred years as many human years; the psalm speaks of seventy or, with strength, eighty. The numbers differ, but both reckon mortal life in a limited span of years.

relationship: Human years set beside eternity
rationale: Sirach reduces human years to a drop or grain beside a day of eternity; the psalm compares a thousand years in God's eyes to a past day or night watch.

relationship: Mercy in view of human frailty
rationale: Sirach's description of short human life leads to the Lord's patience and mercy; the psalm joins His compassion to knowledge that people are dust and pass like grass.

relationship: Atonement and remembrance of mortality
rationale: Sirach connects God's knowledge of the grievous human end with increased atonement; the psalm joins His compassionate atonement to remembrance that people are passing flesh.

relationship: Mercy extending beyond one's neighbor
rationale: Sirach contrasts limited human mercy with the Lord's mercy upon all flesh; the psalm likewise declares Him kind to all, with compassion over all His works. The target concerns this broad scope.

relationship: Divine favor and receptive discipline
rationale: Sirach associates mercy with receiving discipline; Proverbs urges the child not to reject the Lord's correction, because He disciplines the one He loves.

relationship: Giving without reproach
rationale: Sirach forbids adding reproach or hurtful words to a gift; James portrays God's generous giving as without reproach, supplying a positive example of that manner of giving.

relationship: Beneficial words pictured through bodily relief
rationale: Sirach compares a good word's benefit to dew relieving heat; Proverbs compares good words to honeycombs whose sweetness heals life. Both give speech a restorative sensory image.

relationship: Same-chapter union of gracious speech and giving
rationale: The earlier warning forbids hurtful words with gifts and praises a word's value; this verse draws the two together by locating both the good word and good gift in a gracious person.

relationship: The harm of begrudging generosity
rationale: Sirach depicts the distress caused by a grudging gift and graceless reproach; Proverbs warns against a begrudging host and describes the resulting ruin of good words.

relationship: Preparation before speaking
rationale: Sirach requires learning before speech; Proverbs condemns answering a matter before hearing it as foolishness and reproach. This supports the speech clause, not the separate medical advice.

relationship: Self-examination before judgment
rationale: Sirach urges self-examination before visitation and judgment; Paul requires self-examination and says that discerning ourselves would avert judgment, within his specific teaching about the Lord's meal.

relationship: Repentance and inward humbling
rationale: Sirach calls for humility and repentance while sin can be addressed; Joel calls for a whole-hearted return to God and the tearing of hearts. Neither link requires treating illness as a particular sin's result.

relationship: Prompt fulfillment of a vow
rationale: Both warn against delaying payment of a vow. Ecclesiastes explicitly says it is better not to vow than to vow and fail to pay.

relationship: Deliberation before a vow
rationale: Sirach requires preparation before making a vow; Proverbs calls quick consecration a trap when reconsideration comes only after the vow.

relationship: Remembering wrath and retribution
rationale: Sirach directs attention to the coming time of wrath and retribution; Romans warns of stored-up wrath on the day of righteous judgment and repayment according to deeds.

relationship: Preparing for famine during abundance
rationale: Sirach tells the prosperous to remember famine and need; Joseph's plan to reserve food during abundant years for coming famine gives a concrete example of such foresight.

relationship: Uncertainty of changing days
rationale: Sirach emphasizes how quickly circumstances change between morning and evening; Proverbs forbids boasting about tomorrow because the coming day's outcome is unknown.

relationship: Wise caution turning from evil
rationale: Sirach's wise person guards against wrongdoing; Proverbs contrasts the wise person who fears and turns from evil with the self-confident fool who mixes with a lawless person.

relationship: Wisdom expressed in carefully formed sayings
rationale: Sirach associates understanding speech with producing precise proverbs; Ecclesiastes connects wisdom and teaching with an orderly arrangement of proverbs and the search for truthful, upright words.

relationship: Resisting the rule of desire
rationale: Sirach forbids following one's desires and commands restraint of appetites; Galatians similarly warns against fulfilling fleshly desire and contrasts it with walking by the Spirit.

relationship: The danger of yielding to desire
rationale: Sirach warns of the humiliating outcome of satisfying desire; Romans forbids letting sin reign through obedience to bodily desires. The shared issue is surrender to desire, not an identical stated penalty.

relationship: Costly participation in feasting
rationale: Sirach warns that rejoicing in luxury can bind a person to contribute to it; Proverbs likewise warns against stretching oneself over contributions and purchases of meat.

relationship: Feasting and impoverishment
rationale: Sirach warns against impoverishing oneself through borrowed feasts; Proverbs joins a warning about meal contributions to the poverty of the drunkard. Borrowing is Sirach's additional circumstance.

relationship: Drunkenness and poverty
rationale: Sirach says a drunken worker will not become rich; Proverbs likewise predicts poverty for the drunkard. The link concerns the first clause, not the separate warning about despising small things.

relationship: Women, wine, and impaired judgment
rationale: Sirach warns that wine and women lead understanding men astray; the royal instruction warns against giving wealth to women and drinking so as to forget wisdom and fail in judgment.

relationship: Worms as a mortal inheritance
rationale: Both use inheritance language for the association between death and worms. Chapter 10 applies it to human death generally, while this verse concludes a warning about reckless conduct.

relationship: Caution about ready belief
rationale: Sirach criticizes quick trust; Proverbs contrasts the person who believes every word with the resourceful person who reconsiders. This supports the warning about credulity.

relationship: Restrained speech limiting evil
rationale: Sirach says hatred of chatter diminishes evil; Proverbs says much talking does not escape sin and praises sparing one's lips.

relationship: Keeping matters confidential
rationale: Sirach warns against repeating a word; Proverbs contrasts disclosure by a double-tongued person with a faithful person's concealment of matters.

relationship: Discretion about disclosure
rationale: Sirach forbids revealing a matter to friend or enemy unless silence would be sinful; Proverbs praises faithful concealment. Sirach expressly states an exception that the proverb does not discuss.

relationship: Same-chapter consequence of indiscreet disclosure
rationale: The preceding commands forbid repeating and disclosing a word; this verse explains the danger through a hearer who keeps watch and later hates the speaker.

relationship: Allowing a heard matter to remain concealed
rationale: Sirach's instruction to let a heard word die with oneself corresponds to the faithful person's concealment of matters in Proverbs.

relationship: Same-chapter painful images for an unrestrained word
rationale: The word troubling a fool is compared first to labor pains and then to an arrow fixed in flesh. Both images portray the fool's inability to bear a word quietly.

relationship: Same-chapter bodily pain as a speech image
rationale: The arrow and belly image continues the preceding comparison of a fool's distress over a word to childbirth pains; the particular connection is the painful pressure of an uncontained word.

relationship: Personal correction seeking a restored relationship
rationale: Sirach urges questioning a friend to establish what happened and prevent repetition; Matthew directs private reproof of a sinning brother with the aim of gaining him. Sirach additionally warns that the deed may not have occurred.

relationship: Same-chapter questioning of alleged conduct and speech
rationale: The two instructions apply the same cautious questioning first to an alleged deed and then to alleged speech, allowing innocence and seeking to prevent repetition if the report is true.

relationship: Testing reports instead of believing everything
rationale: Sirach warns that slander is frequent and forbids trusting every report; Proverbs contrasts believing every word with thoughtful reconsideration.

relationship: The common danger of stumbling in speech
rationale: Sirach asks who has not sinned with the tongue and allows unintended slips; James says all stumble in many things and makes freedom from stumbling in speech a mark of completeness.

relationship: Lawful correction instead of hostility
rationale: Sirach calls for questioning before threatening and giving place to God's law; Leviticus commands reproof of one's neighbor while forbidding hatred, vengeance, and lasting anger.

relationship: Wisdom as reverence and obedient conduct
rationale: Sirach identifies wisdom with fear of the Lord and doing the law; Job identifies reverence for God with wisdom and abstention from evil with knowledge.

relationship: Distinguishing wisdom from wicked cleverness
rationale: Sirach denies that knowledge of wickedness or sinful counsel is wisdom; James rejects jealous, self-seeking wisdom as earthly and demonic and contrasts it with pure, peaceable wisdom.

relationship: A kind of cleverness unworthy of wisdom's name
rationale: Sirach allows for abhorrent shrewdness; James similarly distinguishes purported wisdom that is earthly and demonic from the pure wisdom from above.

relationship: Same-chapter priority of fear and obedience over cleverness
rationale: The preference for a less knowledgeable but God-fearing person over a lawbreaking expert follows the chapter's definition of wisdom as fear of the Lord and doing the law.

relationship: Same-chapter rejection of unjust shrewdness
rationale: The first clause's precise but unjust shrewdness illustrates the earlier refusal to call knowledge of wickedness wisdom. The link does not resolve the separate clause about twisting matters to bring judgment to light.

relationship: Humble-looking behavior concealing deceit
rationale: Sirach describes gloomy, bowed-down conduct with deceit within; Proverbs describes an enemy's tears and agreeable lips while his heart devises deceit.

relationship: Deceptive outward conduct
rationale: The concealed face and pretended deafness belong to Sirach's deceptive character portrait; Proverbs similarly warns that an enemy's outward entreaties can conceal inward evil.

relationship: Circumstances preventing a sinful act
rationale: Lack of strength prevents sin here, while need prevents it in chapter 20. Sirach 19 adds an evil intention for a future opportunity; that intention is not imputed to the other passage.

relationship: Wisdom visible in the face
rationale: Sirach associates recognizing understanding with the look of a person's face; Ecclesiastes says wisdom lights up the face and contrasts a shameless face.

relationship: Same-chapter expansion of visible character signs
rationale: After appearance and facial expression, the description adds clothing, the grin of the teeth, and one's steps as outward signs by which a person's character is recognized.

relationship: Prudent restraint in speech
rationale: Sirach contrasts an unfitting rebuke with prudent silence; Proverbs praises restraint of a harsh word and says someone who makes himself mute will seem intelligent.

relationship: Reproof preferred to sustained anger
rationale: Sirach prefers rebuke to anger; Leviticus requires reproof of the neighbor while forbidding hatred and remaining angry with one's people.

relationship: Acknowledgment of wrongdoing
rationale: Sirach associates acknowledging fault with preservation from loss; 1 John calls for confession of sins and promises forgiveness and cleansing. The outcomes are stated differently.

relationship: Silence and the appearance of wisdom
rationale: Both sayings associate silence with being regarded as wise or intelligent. Sirach adds the contrast of hatred caused by much chatter.

relationship: Recognizing a time for silence
rationale: Sirach distinguishes inability to answer from knowing the right time to remain silent; Ecclesiastes explicitly gives both silence and speech their proper time.

relationship: Speaking and keeping silent at the proper time
rationale: The wise person's waiting to speak corresponds to Ecclesiastes' recognition of a time to be silent and a time to speak; Sirach contrasts the fool who misses that time.

relationship: The harmful multiplication of words
rationale: Sirach warns that multiplying words brings loathing; Ecclesiastes portrays the fool multiplying words while his own lips drown him. The connection concerns excess speech, not Sirach's separate authority clause.

relationship: Gain that turns into harm
rationale: Sirach allows for a gain that brings loss; Ecclesiastes describes wealth kept to its owner's harm and then lost through a grievous distraction.

relationship: Elevation from lowliness
rationale: Sirach's second clause describes someone lifting his head from lowliness; James promises exaltation to those who humble themselves before the Lord. James supplies the explicitly religious setting.

relationship: Wise words winning favor
rationale: Sirach says the wise person makes himself welcome through words; Ecclesiastes describes a wise person's words as gracious and contrasts the self-destructive lips of a fool.

relationship: A gift or meal spoiled by the giver's disposition
rationale: Sirach rejects a gift whose giver seeks excessive return; Proverbs warns against dining with a begrudging person. Both expose apparent generosity that does not benefit the recipient.

relationship: Same-chapter portrait of an ungenerous giver
rationale: The giver seeking many things for one gift is further portrayed as giving little, reproaching loudly, and demanding repayment almost immediately.

relationship: Same-chapter contrast between complaint and conduct
rationale: The fool complains of having no friend or gratitude after the passage has described gifts demanding excessive return and reproach. The connection places his complaint beside the specific conduct that precedes it.

relationship: Stumbling with the tongue
rationale: Sirach considers a slip of the tongue worse than a slip on the ground; James similarly uses stumbling in speech as an image of human moral failure.

relationship: Same-chapter speech spoiled by poor timing
rationale: The untimely tale associated with a graceless person is followed by the rejected proverb a fool does not speak at its proper time. Both concern inappropriate verbal performance.

relationship: A proverb unfitted to a fool's mouth
rationale: Sirach explains rejection of a fool's proverb through his failure to speak at the proper time; Proverbs also separates a proverb from the mouth of fools without supplying that particular explanation.

relationship: External circumstances restraining sin
rationale: Need prevents sin in this verse, as lack of strength does in chapter 19. Only the earlier passage explicitly adds an intention to do evil when opportunity comes.

relationship: Fearful regard for people causing a fall
rationale: Sirach warns that shame and regard for a foolish person can destroy one's soul; Proverbs describes people tripped up by fear and shame before others, in the setting of failing to report wrongdoing.

relationship: Condemnation of lying speech
rationale: Sirach calls a lie an evil blemish that repeatedly appears in uninstructed speech; Proverbs calls lying lips an abomination to the Lord.

relationship: Destruction overtaking theft and false speech
rationale: Sirach says both theft and persistent lying end in destruction; Zechariah's curse brings death and destruction upon thieves and false swearers. False swearing is the target's particular form of falsehood.

relationship: Falsehood and shame
rationale: Sirach associates a liar's character with dishonor and continuing shame; Proverbs contrasts the righteous person's hatred of an unjust word with the impious person's shame and loss of frankness.

relationship: Speech finding favor with rulers
rationale: Sirach connects wise speech with advancement and pleasing dignitaries; Proverbs says righteous lips are acceptable to a king and that he loves upright words.

relationship: Working the land and receiving food
rationale: Sirach's cultivator raises a heap of grain; Proverbs says the worker of his own land will be filled with loaves. The link concerns cultivation, not the separate clause about pleasing dignitaries.

relationship: Gifts blinding judgment
rationale: Both explicitly say gifts blind the eyes and interfere with right speech or correction. Exodus prohibits receiving such gifts; Sirach illustrates their silencing effect with a muzzle.

relationship: Repeated hidden-wisdom and unseen-treasure saying
rationale: The later passage repeats the question about the benefit of hidden wisdom and unseen treasure, preserving the paired images and the challenge about their usefulness.

relationship: Repeated preference for hiding folly rather than wisdom
rationale: Both passages state the same comparison: the person concealing foolishness is better than the person concealing wisdom.

relationship: Repentance and prayer over committed sin
rationale: Sirach calls for ceasing to add sins and praying concerning earlier ones; Peter likewise tells Simon to repent of his wickedness and plead with the Lord for forgiveness.

relationship: Fleeing sin rather than approaching it
rationale: Sirach commands flight from sin because it attacks and destroys; Paul commands flight from sexual immorality and identifies its harm to one's own body. Sexual immorality is the target's specific case.

relationship: Sin's deadly two-edged blade image
rationale: Sirach compares lawlessness to an incurably wounding two-edged sword; Proverbs uses a two-edged blade for the bitter outcome of involvement with a prostitute and describes the path to death and Hades.

relationship: The destruction of the proud person's house
rationale: Sirach predicts the wasting of the proud person's house; Proverbs explicitly says the Lord pulls down the houses of the insolent.

relationship: The poor person's cry heard by the Lord
rationale: Sirach describes the poor petitioner's words reaching God's ears; the psalm recounts a poor man's cry being heard and his rescue from afflictions.

relationship: Hatred of correction
rationale: Sirach puts hatred of rebuke on the sinner's path and contrasts a receptive fear of God; Proverbs contrasts love of discipline with the foolishness of hating rebukes.

relationship: A house endangered by another's resources
rationale: Sirach likens building with others' money to collecting stones for a storm; Habakkuk condemns accumulating what is not one's own and acquiring evil gain for a house that will suffer shame.

relationship: The lawless as tow consumed by fire
rationale: Both describe lawless people through the image of tow ending in fire. Isaiah adds sparks from their works and the absence of anyone to quench the burning.

relationship: An attractive road ending in Hades
rationale: Sirach's smoothly paved sinners' road ends in the pit of Hades; Proverbs warns of a way that seems upright but ends at the bottom of Hades.

relationship: Wisdom, fear of God, and the law
rationale: Sirach 19 identifies wisdom with fear of the Lord and doing the law; this verse again joins keeping the law with wisdom as the fulfillment of that fear.

relationship: Shrewdness with a harmful character
rationale: The warning that some shrewdness multiplies bitterness corresponds to the earlier statement that there is shrewdness which is an abomination. Both refuse to treat cleverness alone as sufficient wisdom.

relationship: Wise instruction as a spring of life
rationale: Sirach compares the wise person's counsel to a spring of life; Proverbs calls the wise person's law a fountain of life. The life-giving water image is shared.

relationship: Broken pottery and the failure to instruct a fool
rationale: Sirach depicts the fool's inability to retain knowledge as a broken vessel; the next chapter compares teaching a fool to gluing a potsherd together.

relationship: The wise learner receives and increases instruction
rationale: Sirach's knowledgeable hearer praises and adds to a wise word; Proverbs says the wise person responds to reproof with love and becomes wiser when given a starting point. Both contrast receptive wisdom with resistance.

relationship: Grace in an understanding person's speech
rationale: Sirach contrasts the burden of a fool's explanation with grace on an understanding lip; Ecclesiastes likewise calls wise words gracious and contrasts the fool's harmful lips.

relationship: Attentive reception of wise counsel
rationale: Sirach describes an assembly seeking and considering the prudent person's words; Job remembers hearers attending silently to his counsel and awaiting his speech like thirsty earth awaiting rain.

relationship: Contrasting responses to instruction's bonds
rationale: The senseless experience instruction as fetters and handcuffs; chapter 6 tells the learner to accept wisdom's fetters and promises that her bonds will become shelter, glory, and gladness.

relationship: The sound of foolish laughter
rationale: Sirach contrasts a fool's loud laughter with a prudent person's quiet smile; Ecclesiastes likens foolish laughter to crackling thorns beneath a cauldron and calls it futility.

relationship: Instruction worn as a precious ornament
rationale: Instruction is a golden ornament and bracelet for the prudent here; chapter 6 likewise describes wisdom with a golden ornament, glorious clothing, and a crown of rejoicing.

relationship: Restraint when entering another's space
rationale: Sirach contrasts the fool's hurried entrance into a house with an experienced person's reserve; Proverbs advises bringing one's foot rarely to a friend lest the friend become filled with one's presence and respond with hatred.

relationship: Same-chapter restraint at another person's house
rationale: The contrast between hasty entry and experienced reserve is sharpened into the contrast between peering through the door and respectfully standing outside.

relationship: Same-chapter respect for a household's boundary
rationale: Peering into a house and listening at its door are successive examples of uninstructed intrusion; the instructed person stands outside and recognizes the dishonor of such conduct.

relationship: Deliberate assessment of one's words
rationale: Sirach depicts prudent words as weighed in a balance; Proverbs describes the wise heart understanding what comes from its own mouth and carrying discernment on its lips.

relationship: The whisperer's destructive speech
rationale: Sirach condemns the whisperer's self-staining conduct and local hatred; chapter 28 names whispering and double speech as destroyers of peaceful people and causes of unrest.

relationship: Same-chapter repulsive images of laziness
rationale: The comparison of the lazy person to a filthy stone is followed by a comparison to dung. The two images portray others' disgust without requiring a claim that the objects are identical.

relationship: Same-chapter disgust at laziness
rationale: The dung image and the hand shaken after contact continue the preceding filthy-stone image and the public dishonor of the lazy person.

relationship: Parental sorrow over an uninstructed child
rationale: Sirach calls begetting an uninstructed child a father's shame; Proverbs says a father does not rejoice over an uneducated son. The connection concerns that clause, not the separate statement about a daughter.

relationship: A child's conduct affecting the parent
rationale: Sirach contrasts the prudent daughter with one who brings parental grief; Proverbs similarly contrasts a wise son who gladdens his father with a foolish son who grieves his mother. The target does not explain inheriting a husband.

relationship: A wife's harmful conduct within marriage
rationale: Sirach describes a shameless woman's dishonor to father and husband; Proverbs contrasts a courageous wife with an evil-doing woman who destroys a man like a worm in wood.

relationship: Recognizing the proper occasion for mourning and joy
rationale: Sirach compares untimely discourse to music during mourning; Ecclesiastes distinguishes times for weeping and laughing, mourning and dancing. This concerns appropriate occasions, not Sirach's separate commendation of discipline.

relationship: The fool and broken pottery as a learning image
rationale: Teaching the fool is compared to repairing a potsherd, corresponding to the earlier description of the fool's inward parts as a broken vessel that cannot retain knowledge.

relationship: Speech wasted on a foolish hearer
rationale: Sirach's drowsy fool fails to take in what has been said; Proverbs forbids speaking into a fool's ears because he will sneer at intelligent words. The failures differ, but both concern an unreceptive hearer.

relationship: The dead person's rest tempering grief
rationale: Sirach gives the dead person's rest as a reason for gentler weeping; chapter 38 similarly calls for comfort and the resting of remembrance when the dead person rests. This addresses the consolation clause, not the whole comparison with a fool.

relationship: Seven days of mourning
rationale: Sirach names seven days as the period of mourning for the dead; Genesis records Joseph mourning his father for seven days. The narrative illustrates that duration, not the lifelong grief over a fool.

relationship: Avoiding fruitless speech with a fool
rationale: Sirach warns against multiplying words with someone without understanding; Proverbs likewise forbids speaking into a fool's ears because intelligent words will meet contempt.

relationship: The fool as an exceptionally heavy burden
rationale: Sirach calls the fool heavier than lead; Proverbs calls a fool's anger heavier than stone and sand. The materials and scope differ, but the disproportionate weight image is shared.

relationship: The fool outweighing heavy materials
rationale: Sirach finds sand, salt, and iron easier to bear than an uncomprehending person; Proverbs similarly compares stone and sand with the still heavier anger of a fool.

relationship: Wise understanding pictured as a stable building
rationale: Sirach compares a heart established on counsel to a fitted wooden bond that withstands shaking; Jesus compares hearing and doing His words to a prudent builder whose house withstands wind and water.

relationship: Same-chapter architectural images of a firm heart
rationale: The heart established through understanding is depicted first through a fitted structural bond and then through an ornament on a polished wall. Both images concern a heart made firm by thought or counsel.

relationship: Folly exposed by a destructive storm
rationale: Sirach likens a fearful heart resting on foolish thought to stakes unable to withstand wind; Jesus compares failure to act on His words to a foolish builder whose house falls when the storm strikes.

relationship: Reproach and the breaking of friendship
rationale: Sirach says reproaching a friend drives friendship away like stones scattering birds; Proverbs contrasts concealing wrongdoings to seek friendship with exposing them in a way that separates friends.

relationship: The possibility of reconciliation after hostility
rationale: Sirach tells someone who has drawn a sword against a friend not to despair of a way back; Jesus directs a person whose brother has a grievance to seek reconciliation before presenting a gift.

relationship: Disclosure of secrets as a grave breach of friendship
rationale: Sirach distinguishes reparable hostile speech from breaches that drive a friend away, including disclosed secrets; chapter 27 likewise allows reconciliation after abuse but treats betrayed secrets as destroying trust and hope.

relationship: Friendship maintained in adversity
rationale: Sirach urges faithfulness to a neighbor in poverty and affliction; Proverbs calls for a friend at all times and for brothers to be useful in need.

relationship: Inflammatory words preceding conflict
rationale: Sirach says insults precede bloodshed as smoke precedes fire; Proverbs says a painful word stirs up anger and contrasts a yielding answer that turns wrath away.

relationship: Refusing to abandon a friend
rationale: Sirach declares willingness to shelter a friend without hiding from him; Proverbs directly forbids abandoning one's friend or an ancestral friend.

relationship: Prayer for a guard over the mouth
rationale: Both ask for a guard upon the mouth and protection around the lips. Sirach describes a skillful seal, while the psalm describes a restraining door.

relationship: Prayer against being led into sinful speech
rationale: Following the request to guard the mouth, Sirach asks God not to abandon him to their counsel or let him fall through them; the psalm also joins a guarded mouth to prayer against a heart turned toward wicked words.

relationship: Welcoming corrective discipline
rationale: Sirach seeks discipline over thought and heart so that errors are not spared; the psalm welcomes a righteous person's merciful discipline and correction.

relationship: Sin, stumbling, and enemies' gloating
rationale: Sirach prays that multiplying sins not cause a fall before gloating enemies; the psalm joins concern over lawlessness to the plea that enemies not rejoice when the speaker's feet are shaken.

relationship: Rejecting haughty eyes
rationale: Sirach asks God not to give him haughty eyes; the psalmist declares that his eyes were not raised high and his heart was not exalted.

relationship: Prayer for desire to be redirected
rationale: Sirach asks that desire be turned away; the psalm asks God to bend the heart away from greed and turn the eyes from futility toward His way.

relationship: Resisting bodily and sexual appetites
rationale: Sirach asks not to be overcome by belly and sexual appetite; Romans forbids revelry, drunkenness, and sexual promiscuity and rejects provision for fleshly desires.

relationship: Guarded speech preserving life
rationale: Sirach promises that the keeper of mouth-discipline will not be caught; Proverbs says guarding one's mouth preserves life and contrasts rash lips.

relationship: A sinner trapped through speech
rationale: Both explicitly describe a sinner falling into a trap through the lips. Sirach additionally names abusive and proud speakers as stumbling through them.

relationship: Restraint from habitual oaths
rationale: Sirach warns against accustoming the mouth to oaths; James commands plain yes and no instead of swearing and connects the warning with judgment.

relationship: Invoking God's name and accountability for sin
rationale: Sirach warns that continual swearing and invoking the name will not leave a person cleansed from sin; Exodus refuses acquittal to someone who takes the Lord's name in vain. The target specifically addresses vain invocation.

relationship: False swearing bringing calamity upon a house
rationale: Sirach warns that vain or offending oaths fill a house with calamities; Zechariah describes the curse entering and destroying the false swearer's house.

relationship: Rejecting crude and foolish speech
rationale: Sirach forbids making crude ignorance a habit of the mouth because sinful speech lies in it; Ephesians rejects shamefulness, foolish talk, and coarse joking as unfitting.

relationship: Cursing the day of one's birth
rationale: Sirach describes birth-regret and a curse on one's birth day as a possible result of public foolishness; Job actually curses his birth day in suffering. The particular expression is shared, while its circumstances differ.

relationship: Same-chapter harmful habits of speech
rationale: The warning against habitual crude speech is extended to a person habituated to reproach who remains uninstructed. Both focus on speech becoming an entrenched habit.

relationship: Sexual misconduct pictured as consuming fire
rationale: Sirach places the heated soul's consuming fire beside the sexually immoral man's kindled fire; Proverbs compares involvement with a married woman to carrying fire or walking on burning coals without escaping injury.

relationship: The adulterer relying on darkness for concealment
rationale: Both give the adulterer's claim that no one will see him in darkness. Job also describes concealing the face; Sirach exposes the further mistaken assumption that God will not remember.

relationship: God's eyes observing every human way
rationale: Sirach denies that hidden places conceal misconduct from the Lord's eyes; Proverbs says a man's ways are before God's eyes and that He watches all his tracks, in a warning about another woman.

relationship: Divine knowledge before formation
rationale: Sirach states God's knowledge of all things before their creation; God's declaration that He knows Jeremiah before forming him supplies a particular instance of prior knowledge.

relationship: Sexual wrongdoing overtaken by its consequences
rationale: Sirach's adulterer is seized where he did not expect it; Proverbs describes lawless acts hunting a person and the cords of sins binding him, within its warning about another woman.

relationship: A wife joining another man during marriage
rationale: Sirach condemns the wife leaving her husband and presenting another man's heir; Romans describes a woman belonging to another man while her husband lives as adulterous. The heir is Sirach's additional detail.

relationship: Adultery as disobedience to God's law
rationale: Sirach explicitly names the woman's adultery as disobedience to the Most High's law; the native Exodus 20:13 gives the command against adultery.

relationship: Same-chapter elaboration of visitation upon offspring
rationale: The announcement of visitation upon the woman's children is followed by the image of children without a spreading root and branches without fruit. The later verse develops this stated consequence.

relationship: Unlawful offspring described by unstable roots and fruit
rationale: Sirach describes the children through roots that do not spread and fruitless branches; Wisdom likewise uses insecure roots and useless fruit for offspring from unlawful unions.

relationship: Adultery's lasting reproach
rationale: Sirach predicts an unerased reproach and cursed memory for the adulterous woman; Proverbs describes the adulterer's dishonor and says his reproach will never be wiped away.

relationship: The excellence of fearing God and the sweetness of His judgments
rationale: Sirach praises fear of the Lord and the sweetness of attending to His commandments; the psalm places enduring fear of the Lord beside judgments sweeter than honey and the reward of keeping them.

relationship: Personified wisdom speaking publicly
rationale: Sirach introduces Wisdom praising herself among her people; Proverbs likewise presents Wisdom at public ways and gates, sending her voice to human beings.

relationship: Wisdom's public address
rationale: Wisdom opens her mouth before the Most High's assembly in Sirach; Proverbs presents her speaking at public gathering places to human beings. The audiences differ, but the speaking personification is shared.

relationship: Wisdom coming forth from God
rationale: Sirach has Wisdom come from the Most High's mouth; Wisdom of Solomon calls her a breath of God's power and a pure outflow of His glory. Both portray her origin through an image of proceeding from God.

relationship: The pillar of cloud
rationale: Wisdom locates her throne in a pillar of cloud; Exodus describes God's guidance of Israel in a pillar of cloud. The connection is the distinctive image of divine presence, without claiming that Exodus explicitly names Wisdom.

relationship: Wisdom associated with the cosmic heights and depths
rationale: Sirach's Wisdom traverses heaven and the abyss; Proverbs describes her before the deeps and present with God as heaven and the world's springs are established.

relationship: Wisdom's universal reach and rule
rationale: Sirach describes Wisdom's possession extending through sea, earth, and every people; Wisdom of Solomon says she reaches from end to end and governs all things well.

relationship: Same-chapter search for a dwelling answered
rationale: Wisdom's search for rest and an inheritance in which to lodge receives the particular answer of the Creator settling her tent in Jacob and assigning her Israel as an inheritance.

relationship: Divine instruction entrusted particularly to Israel
rationale: Wisdom is commanded to dwell in Jacob and receive Israel as her inheritance; the psalm describes God's word and judgments being given to Jacob and Israel in a way not granted to every nation. Sirach 24:23 identifies the discourse with the law.

relationship: Wisdom created before the age
rationale: Both personifications speak of the Lord creating or founding Wisdom before the age. Proverbs expands this into a description of Wisdom before the earth, deeps, mountains, and hills.

relationship: Zion as the chosen sacred dwelling
rationale: Wisdom's ministry in the holy tent and establishment in Zion correspond to the psalm's selection of Zion as the Lord's dwelling and its mention of His priests. The psalm speaks of the Lord's choice, not a separate statement by Wisdom.

relationship: The chosen place of dwelling in Zion
rationale: Wisdom describes being settled in the beloved city, Jerusalem; the psalm names Zion as the place the Lord selected for His dwelling and rest.

relationship: Jacob as the Lord's portion and inheritance
rationale: Sirach's description of the people as the Lord's portion and inheritance directly corresponds to Deuteronomy's naming of Jacob and Israel in those terms.

relationship: Flourishing like a cedar of Lebanon
rationale: Wisdom's tall cedar of Lebanon image corresponds to the psalm's comparison of the righteous person's flourishing with a cedar in Lebanon.

relationship: The flourishing olive-tree image
rationale: Sirach compares Wisdom to a stately olive among other trees; the psalmist compares himself to a fruitful olive in God's house. The shared image concerns flourishing, while the subjects and settings differ.

relationship: Fragrance using the sanctuary's incense ingredients
rationale: Sirach's description of Wisdom's scent names galbanum, onycha, stacte, and frankincense; Exodus lists these ingredients for holy incense placed before the testimonies in the tent.

relationship: Wisdom pictured as a tree
rationale: Wisdom's spreading terebinth branches form a tree image for her glory and grace; Proverbs likewise calls Wisdom a tree of life for those who hold her fast.

relationship: Vine blossom as an image of flourishing
rationale: Wisdom describes her gracious growth and blossoms through a vine; Hosea's restoration imagery similarly culminates in blossoming like a vine. Hosea applies the image to restored Israel rather than to personified Wisdom.

relationship: Wisdom inviting people to eat
rationale: Both personified Wisdom discourses invite hearers to come and receive nourishment: Sirach offers her produce, while Proverbs offers her bread and mixed wine and calls for leaving foolishness.

relationship: Instruction sweeter than honey
rationale: Wisdom calls her memory and inheritance sweeter than honey and honeycomb; the psalmist calls God's sayings sweeter than honey and honeycomb. Sirach's identification with the law in 24:23 makes the instructional connection explicit.

relationship: Contrasting hunger and thirst language
rationale: Sirach's Wisdom says those eating and drinking her will continue to hunger and thirst; Jesus, the bread of life, promises no hunger or thirst to those who come and believe. The paired images are close, while the stated outcomes contrast.

relationship: Obedience, freedom from shame, and avoidance of sin
rationale: Wisdom promises that obedience avoids shame and working in her avoids sin; the psalm joins attention to God's commandments with freedom from shame and hiding His sayings in the heart to avoid sinning.

relationship: Direct correspondence in the law-as-inheritance wording
rationale: Sirach identifies the discourse with the law Moses commanded as an inheritance for Jacob's assemblies, closely reproducing the wording of Deuteronomy 33:4.

relationship: Eden's rivers in the picture of abundant wisdom
rationale: Sirach names the Pishon and Tigris in its flood image for wisdom; Genesis names both among the rivers flowing from Eden. The connection identifies the particular rivers, without making Genesis itself an allegory of wisdom.

relationship: The Jordan at harvest as an abundance image
rationale: Sirach compares overflowing understanding to the Jordan in harvest days; Joshua explicitly describes the Jordan overflowing its bank during wheat harvest.

relationship: The named river Gihon
rationale: Sirach's comparison of instruction to the Gihon participates in the surrounding series of named rivers; Genesis identifies Gihon as one of Eden's rivers. The light and vintage comparisons remain Sirach's own imagery.

relationship: Wisdom beyond complete human discovery
rationale: Sirach says neither the first nor the last traced Wisdom fully; Job describes wisdom as hidden from human beings while God knows its place.

relationship: Same-chapter depths explaining Wisdom's untraceability
rationale: Wisdom's thought growing abundant from the sea and her counsel from a great abyss develop the preceding statement that neither first nor last has traced her fully. The connection concerns the explicitly stated limits of discovery.

relationship: Speech or teaching pictured as flowing water
rationale: Sirach's speaker compares himself to a river channel watering a garden; Proverbs compares a word in the heart to deep water and a springing river, a fountain of life.

relationship: Same-chapter expansion of the teaching-water image
rationale: The channel and garden watercourse of the preceding verse grow into a river and sea as the speaker waters his garden. This is the deliberate expansion of the same water image.

relationship: Instruction as illuminating light
rationale: Sirach promises to make instruction shine like dawn; Proverbs calls the law's commandment a lamp and light and joins it with correction and discipline.

relationship: Teaching preserved for future generations
rationale: Sirach's speaker promises to leave teaching for generations of ages; the psalm describes transmitting God's testimony and law so that children yet to be born will teach their own children.

relationship: Repeated declaration of labor for others
rationale: Both statements expressly say the speaker has labored not for himself alone but for others seeking wisdom or instruction.

relationship: The beauty of brothers dwelling in harmony
rationale: Sirach includes harmony among brothers among the relationships beautiful before God and people; the psalm praises brothers dwelling together as good and delightful.

relationship: Learning in youth for wisdom in old age
rationale: The question about finding in old age what was not gathered in youth corresponds to the earlier instruction to choose discipline in youth and find wisdom until the hair is gray.

relationship: Wisdom and knowledge associated with long life
rationale: Sirach calls judgment and counsel fitting for gray-haired elders; Job associates wisdom with much time and knowledge with a long life.

relationship: Expectation of wisdom in age, with a qualification
rationale: Sirach calls wisdom fitting for the old and thought and counsel fitting for the honored; Elihu recounts expecting many years to bring wisdom, then qualifies this by denying that elders necessarily know judgment.

relationship: Old age as a crown associated with reverence or righteousness
rationale: Sirach calls long experience the old person's crown and fear of the Lord his boast; Proverbs calls old age a crown of boasting found in righteous ways.

relationship: Rejoicing in one's children
rationale: Sirach includes a person rejoicing in children among the happy; Proverbs describes parental rejoicing over a wise son and urges the child to gladden father and mother. The enemy's fall is a separate clause.

relationship: The good wife and her husband's happiness
rationale: Sirach calls living with an understanding wife happy; chapter 26 similarly calls the good wife's husband happy and describes the gladness she brings. The target supports the marital clause.

relationship: Happiness in finding understanding
rationale: Sirach calls the finder of prudence happy; Proverbs blesses the person who finds wisdom and sees good sense. This supports the first of the verse's two commendations.

relationship: Fear of the Lord as wisdom's foundation
rationale: Sirach says that even a finder of wisdom is not above the person who fears the Lord; Proverbs makes fear of the Lord wisdom's beginning, connecting the two while giving fear a foundational role.

relationship: The preeminence of fearing the Lord
rationale: The statement that fear of the Lord surpasses everything corresponds to its earlier description as the crown of wisdom, making peace and healing flourish.

relationship: Preference for harsh surroundings over a harmful marriage
rationale: Sirach prefers dwelling with a lion and dragon to an evil woman; Proverbs prefers desert dwelling to a battling, talkative, quick-tempered woman. Both express the comparison through an undesirable alternative dwelling.

relationship: Same-chapter description of a husband's distress
rationale: The husband's involuntary bitter groaning among neighbors is further characterized in the chapter's description of an evil wife as a humbled heart, gloomy face, and wounded heart.

relationship: A difficult marriage compared to adverse physical conditions
rationale: Sirach compares a talkative wife with a sandy ascent beneath an old person's feet; Proverbs compares an abusive wife with wintry drops driving a man from his house. The comparisons and descriptions of the wife differ.

relationship: Resisting desire aroused by beauty
rationale: Both warn against being overcome by desire for a woman's beauty. Proverbs adds being hunted by one's eyes and seized by her eyelids.

relationship: A harmful wife portrayed through bodily damage
rationale: Sirach describes an evil wife through a wounded heart, slack hands, and paralyzed knees; Proverbs likens a woman doing evil to a worm in wood destroying a man.

relationship: An interpretation of sin and mortality in the Eden narrative
rationale: Sirach traces the beginning of sin and human death to the woman; God's sentence on Adam in Genesis connects his listening to his wife and eating with his eventual return to earth. Genesis also names Adam's own act of eating.

relationship: Contrast with the marital bond expressed as shared flesh
rationale: Sirach's instruction to cut the wife off from one's flesh reverses the unity expressed when Genesis calls the woman flesh of the man's flesh and the married pair one flesh. The target explains the marital image, not a rule endorsing Sirach's stated condition.
